meta.title: Who really said "We only have to be lucky once. You will have to be lucky always"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Thatcher. These are the IRA’s words, from the statement claiming the 1984 Brighton bombing — a threat to her, not a maxim by her.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We only have to be lucky once. You will have to be lucky always'?
meta.ogDescription: The line comes from the Provisional IRA statement claiming the Brighton hotel bombing of 12 October 1984. It was aimed at Thatcher.

answer.label: Not Thatcher — the IRA’s threat to her
answer.sourceLine: These are not Margaret Thatcher’s words. They come from the statement the Provisional IRA issued on 12 October 1984, hours after its bomb tore through the Grand Hotel in Brighton during the Conservative Party conference, killing five people and narrowly missing Thatcher herself. The line is a threat addressed to her. Quote Investigator ↗ reproduces the Associated Press report of that day, and Wikipedia prints the IRA Army Council statement in full ↗; Wikiquote files it among quotes about Thatcher ↗, not by her.

source.heading: The statement

docMeta.dd: IRA Army Council statement claiming the Brighton bombing
Associated Press, 12 October 1984 — carried e.g. in The Indiana Gazette, p. 1
Margaret Thatcher, who survived the attack on the Grand Hotel, Brighton

source.excerpt: The IRA claims responsibility for the detonation of 100lb of gelignite in Brighton against the British cabinet and Tory warmongers. Thatcher will now realise that Britain cannot occupy our country, torture our prisoners and shoot our people in their own streets and get away with it. Today we were unlucky, but remember we have only to be lucky once, you will have to be lucky always. Give Ireland peace and there will be no war.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reproduces the Associated Press report of 12 October 1984 carrying the statement, and notes it was signed “P. O’Neill,” the pseudonym long used for IRA communiqués.

Wikipedia’s account of the Brighton hotel bombing ↗ prints the IRA Army Council statement in full, citing Rory Carroll’s 2023 history of the attack, pp. 227–228. The wording matches the AP text to within punctuation.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its “Quotes about Thatcher” section, attributed to the IRA — it appears nowhere in the sections of her own words.

Quote Investigator also records the modern misreading directly: a 2022 post it quotes describes the threat circulating on social media as an inspirational Thatcher quote, reworded to “We only need to be lucky once. You need to be lucky every time.”
We did not read the 1984 Associated Press dispatch or Carroll’s book ourselves. Two independent secondary sources print substantially the same text, and neither attributes it to Thatcher.
source.excerptNote: Two slightly different transcriptions are in circulation: the Associated Press report Quote Investigator quotes reads “remember, we have only to be lucky once: You will have to be lucky always,” while Wikipedia’s text has “remember we have only to be lucky once, you will have to be lucky always.” Both begin “we have only to be lucky once”; the poster version’s “we only have to” is a later smoothing.
source.rightsNote: The statement was issued and published in 1984, more than half a century after the 1931 cut-off for the United States public domain, so it is not public domain. We name no rights holder: it was issued pseudonymously by a proscribed organisation, and who if anyone holds rights in it is not something we can establish. Treat it as uncleared.

author.name: The Provisional IRA
author.heading: About the Provisional IRA
author.metaLine: Irish republican paramilitary organisation · active 1969–2005 · statement issued 12 October 1984
author.bio: The Provisional Irish Republican Army waged an armed campaign against British rule in Northern Ireland from 1969 until its 2005 order to end operations. The Brighton bombing of October 1984 was its attempt to kill the British cabinet, and the statement claiming it was issued by the IRA Army Council under the pseudonym “P. O’Neill.” These words are its words — a fact the quote-poster version of them entirely erases.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is the starkest reversal in our collection: a threat against a prime minister, sold back to the public as her own motivational maxim.

items.tag: Said to her, not by her
items.why: The words were written by the organisation that had just tried to kill her, and were addressed to her. Wikiquote ↗ lists them among quotes about Thatcher and attributes them to the IRA.
Reworded to “We only need to be lucky once. You need to be lucky every time” and set over a landscape photograph, as Quote Investigator records ↗. Removing the bombing removes the entire meaning.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are the Provisional IRA’s, issued on 12 October 1984 to claim the Brighton bombing and to promise Thatcher another attempt — as the full statement makes plain ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: At 2:54 on the morning of 12 October 1984, a long-delay bomb planted weeks earlier in room 629 brought down part of the Grand Hotel in Brighton, where the Conservative Party conference was staying. Five people were killed, including the MP Sir Anthony Berry, and more than thirty were injured. Thatcher was awake and still working when it went off. She was unhurt, and gave her close-of-conference speech at two o’clock that afternoon.

The statement issued later that day was not a boast about resilience. It was a claim of responsibility and a warning that the attempt would be repeated — which is precisely the meaning that vanishes when the sentence is lifted out and captioned with her name.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator ↗ shows the asymmetry it expresses was already a stock figure of speech before 1984: a 1982 North Carolina newspaper quoted a wildlife officer on poachers — “Poachers have to be lucky all of the time. We only have to be lucky once to catch them” — and James Grady’s novel Runner in the Street, published by July 1984, gives a detective almost the same sentence.
That prior history is why the wording drifts so easily, and why the version now attached to Thatcher matches neither of the 1984 transcriptions.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator reproduces the Associated Press report of 12 October 1984 carrying the IRA statement "Today we were unlucky, but remember, we have only to be lucky once: You will have to be lucky always. Give Ireland peace and there will be no war," notes it was signed P. O’Neill, gives 1982 and 1984 precursors, and records the line circulating in 2022 as an inspirational Margaret Thatcher quote.

Wikipedia prints the IRA Army Council statement of 12 October 1984 in full, including "Today we were unlucky, but remember we have only to be lucky once, you will have to be lucky always," citing Carroll 2023 pp. 227-228; and records that five people were killed, including MP Sir Anthony Berry, and Thatcher was uninjured.

Wikiquote lists "Today we were unlucky, but remember we only have to be lucky once - you will have to be lucky always" in its Quotes about Thatcher section, attributed to an IRA statement following the Brighton hotel bombing.
Wikipedia gives the Provisional IRA as active 1969-2005 and records that on 28 July 2005 it declared an end to the armed campaign, ordering volunteers to end all paramilitary activity.
